Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications. The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx. GERD affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs). Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection.

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) in children is very common and refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus. This is often physiological and managed conservatively. In contrast, GER disease (GERD) is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management. Apart from abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, other factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia. The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation. Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD. The following review focuses on up-to-date information regarding of the pathogenesis, diagnostic evaluation and management of GERD in children.

Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting. In this review, we discuss clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms, including proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists.

data.narrative: GERD is a condition where stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, causing symptoms or complications [18#0]. The typical symptoms are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the throat [18#1]. GERD can affect quality of life and may lead to more serious problems including inflammation of the esophagus, narrowing of the esophagus, and a condition called Barrett esophagus, which can be a precursor to esophageal cancer [18#2]. Risk factors for GERD include problems with the esophageal lining's defense, impaired movement and clearance of the esophagus and stomach, and anatomical defects such as hiatal hernia [19#3]. In children, GERD symptoms can be varied and nonspecific, making careful diagnostic evaluation important [19#4]. Symptoms that may be related to GERD are among the most commonly reported complaints in outpatient primary care visits [20#5].

data.narrative: The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the throat [18#0]. GERD happens when stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, causing discomfort or complications [18#1]. It can lower quality of life and may lead to inflammation of the esophagus, narrowing of the esophagus, or Barrett esophagus, which can precede esophageal cancer [18#2]. Symptoms possibly caused by GERD are among the most common reasons people visit their primary care providers [20#3]. In children, reflux is often normal and managed without medication, but GERD is a less common, more serious form that causes troublesome symptoms [19#4]. Risk factors for GERD in children include a hiatal hernia, weak esophageal lining, and problems with how the esophagus and stomach move and clear food [19#5]. In young children, the signs of GERD can be varied and unclear, so careful evaluation is needed [19#6]. Long-term use of the most common GERD medications, called proton-pump inhibitors, carries risks including bone fractures, kidney disease, pneumonia, and intestinal infection [18#7]. The condition is known by several names in medical records, including Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [1], Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) [2], and Gastroesophageal Reflux [3]. Multiple clinical trials have studied GERD treatments, including famotidine for non-erosive disease [4], pantoprazole for acid reflux symptoms in adults [7], endoscopic fundoplication as a placebo-controlled procedure [16], on-demand treatment [13], and the natural history of reflux in children and adolescents [10]. Several publications address GERD, identified by PMID 29132520 [5], PMID 33351044 [8], PMID 36170502 [11], PMID 37034973 [14], and PMID 37516506 [17]. Additional published reviews carry the title Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [6][9][15], and one focuses on what is new in childhood GERD [12].
